summary: Octenidine (octenidine dihydrochloride) is a broad-spectrum topical antiseptic, usually formulated as a 0.1% solution often combined with 2% phenoxyethanol. As a cationic bispyridine surfactant it binds to the negatively charged cell membranes of bacteria, fungi and some enveloped viruses, disrupting them and producing a bactericidal/fungicidal effect with good activity against Gram-positive and Gram-negative organisms (including MRSA) and good persistence on skin. It is used for antiseptic skin and mucous-membrane preparation before procedures, for cleansing and decolonisation, wound antisepsis, and as a mouthwash for oral hygiene. It is for external/topical use only and must not be injected or forced under pressure into closed tissue spaces, because cases of serious tissue damage (oedema, necrosis) have been reported when octenidine was applied under pressure to deep wounds without allowing drainage. Octenidine is essentially not systemically absorbed; it is not FDA-approved as a drug but is widely used in Europe and elsewhere per manufacturer/SmPC labelling.

moa: Octenidine is a positively charged (cationic) bispyridine surfactant. It binds electrostatically to the negatively charged components of microbial cell envelopes (phospholipids and polysaccharides of the cell wall and membrane). This binding disrupts membrane integrity and essential membrane functions, causing leakage of cell contents and microbial death. It has broad bactericidal activity against Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria (including MRSA), fungicidal activity against yeasts, and activity against some enveloped viruses. It binds to skin and mucosa to give a persistent (residual) antiseptic effect and is not appreciably absorbed systemically.

preg: Systemic absorption after topical use is negligible, so topical octenidine is generally considered low-risk in pregnancy. Avoid extensive or repeated mucosal application unless clearly needed.
lact: Negligible systemic absorption makes topical use generally compatible with breastfeeding. Avoid applying to the nipple/areola before feeding, and clean the area beforehand if it has been treated.
renal: Not applicable - topical octenidine is essentially not absorbed systemically.
hepatic: Not applicable - topical octenidine is essentially not absorbed systemically.

moderate: Anionic surfactants (e.g. some soaps, sodium lauryl sulfate) - may inactivate the cationic antiseptic; rinse off before use
minor: Iodine-containing antiseptics (e.g. PVP-iodine) - avoid using on the same area (can cause brown-violet discoloration/reduced effect)
interactions.food: Not applicable; oral rinse should not be swallowed
interactions.diagnostics: No significant systemic laboratory interference with topical use

counsel: This is an antiseptic for the skin, mouth or wounds - it is for use on the outside of the body only and must never be injected
Apply to clean skin, let it wet the area fully and stay on for the recommended time; do not let it pool under your body
If using the mouthwash, rinse and spit it out - do not swallow; your teeth/tongue may temporarily stain
Avoid getting it in the eyes or ears; rinse with water if this happens
Stop and seek advice if you get marked stinging, rash or swelling

pearls: Cationic bispyridine antiseptic with broad bactericidal/fungicidal activity (including MRSA) and good skin persistence
EXTERNAL USE ONLY - never inject or apply under pressure into deep/closed wounds (risk of tissue oedema and necrosis); ensure drainage
Avoid pooling under the body (chemical burns) and avoid the eyes and inner ear
Inactivated by anionic surfactants (soaps) and incompatible with iodine antiseptics on the same site
Not FDA-approved as a drug; widely used in Europe/Asia per manufacturer/SmPC labelling. Negligible systemic absorption
missed: Not applicable - octenidine is a topical antiseptic used as needed for skin, wound or oral antisepsis rather than a scheduled systemic medicine.
overdose: Systemic overdose is not expected with correct topical use because absorption is negligible. Accidental ingestion of large amounts of an oral rinse may cause gastrointestinal upset; manage supportively and seek advice from a poison-control centre. Serious local harm follows incorrect injection or pressurised deep-wound application, which requires surgical assessment, drainage and debridement of affected tissue.
